title: Peanuts (the comic) Part II
summary: Part two of a two-part Peanuts episode. The hosts continue with Snoopy's alter egos and family, Woodstock's name and generational symbolism, Peppermint Patty, Marcy, and Sally, the Vietnam-era strips, the Title IX strips, and Franklin, the first Black Peanuts character, created after a 1968 letter from teacher Harriet Glickman and advice from Kenneth Kelly. They cover Pig Pen, Sally's school-building talks, the minimalist strip style, the Midwest setting, the 1954 adult-legs golf strip, A Charlie Brown Christmas, Schulz's essential tremor and colon cancer, his death in February 2000, the posthumous reprints, and the 2022 tributes. The episode closes with a listener mail message from Olivia in Ottawa.

segments.title: Opening and Snoopy background
segments.summary: The hosts recap part one and introduce Snoopy's origins (based on Schulz's dog Spike, and the name from his mother), his many alter egos such as the Flying Ace, and the Royal Guardsman novelty hit.

segments.title: Vietnam War and Snoopy
segments.summary: Schulz gave the Air Force approval to use Snoopy as a mascot in Vietnam, then grew anti-war and used the Flying Ace strips to criticize the war, including strips about the draft.

segments.title: Spike, Joe Cool, and Snoopy trivia
segments.summary: Discussion of Snoopy's siblings including Spike, the Joe Cool alter ego, Joe Grunge, the Snoopy snow cone machine, and Snoop Dogg's nickname.

segments.title: Woodstock's name and generational symbolism
segments.summary: Woodstock was named in a 1970 strip. Michelle Abate's book reads Woodstock as representing the younger generation and hippies. The hosts debate whether that reading is convincing.

segments.title: Peppermint Patty, Marcy, and sexuality speculation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss fan speculation about Peppermint Patty and Marcy's sexuality, Schulz's 1997 remarks that sexuality was not relevant to the children, and Peppermint Patty's name inversions.

segments.title: Title IX and Billie Jean King strips
segments.summary: Schulz drew strips around Title IX, using Peppermint Patty as a stand-in for women athletes, inspired by his friend Billie Jean King. The hosts note the strips are not about her being gay.

segments.title: Peppermint Patty, Marcy, and the other side of town
segments.summary: Peppermint Patty, Marcy, and Franklin attend a different school. Peppermint Patty was raised by her single father, is a tomboy, and is a non-traditional female strip character. Marcy is smart but depicted as unintelligent in some ways, has no last name, and is sometimes read as Asian American.

segments.title: Franklin, the first Black Peanuts character
segments.summary: Harriet Glickman wrote to Schulz in 1968 after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination asking for a Black character. Schulz was initially hesitant, then took advice from Kenneth Kelly to introduce Franklin casually. The beach strip where they meet is described, and Schulz faced hostile editors and threatened to quit. Franklin was later given the last name Armstrong after cartoonist Rob Armstrong.

segments.title: Pig Pen, Sally, and other minor characters
segments.summary: Pig Pen's first strip in 1954, his self-contentment, his appearance in Dave Did the Math statistics, and the Grateful Dead's Pigpen connection. Sally's crush on Linus and her talks with the school building.

segments.title: Minimalist style and Midwest setting
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the spare four-panel style and the boundless universe, then the presumed Midwest setting based on seasons, with Schulz's roots in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area and his later move to Santa Rosa, California.

segments.title: Adults in Peanuts and A Charlie Brown Christmas
segments.summary: The Peanuts world has almost no adults. A 1954 Sunday strip shows adult legs during a golf game with Lucy. The hosts recall A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965), its jazz soundtrack, lack of laugh track, and the Linus and Lucy song, plus the Charlie Brown Christmas tree product.

segments.title: Schulz retirement, essential tremor, and death
segments.summary: Schulz announced retirement in December 1999 after a terminal colon cancer diagnosis. He had essential tremor from 1981, visible in the progressively squiggly line. He died February 12, 2000, at 77, and the family stopped new strips, so only reprints appear now.

segments.title: Legacy and 2022 tributes
segments.summary: Peanuts is described as a billion-dollar brand and Bill Watterson credits Schulz for merchandising. Other cartoonists paid tribute on November 26, 2022, including Gil Thorp, Curtis, Garfield, and Mary Worth, and the Charles Schulz Museum site has links. The hosts close by reading the first Peanuts strip.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh recommends reading Peanuts strips and makes a closing remark.

segments.title: Listener mail from Olivia
segments.summary: Olivia from Ottawa, Ontario, writes that the podcast has been a steady presence in her life and that she and her long-distance partner listen together.
